scenes.narration: Meet Dana. She runs a shift at a warehouse in Ohio. This spring, the robots arrived. They don't take a salary. They don't take vacations. They never ask for a raise. And the warehouse is making more money than ever. So Dana has a question. If the robots do the work, who gets the money? Here's a clue. In America, the share of business output paid to workers has just hit the lowest level on record. So the real question about AI may not be, will I keep my job? It may be, do I own any of the machines?

scenes.narration: When Dana's dad started on the loading dock, back in the seventies, workers got about fifty-eight dollars of that bill.
Today, they get about fifty-one. And the owners' slice, profit after tax, has roughly doubled.

A few dollars doesn't sound like much. But this bill stands for the whole American economy. By our rough math, that gap is worth more than two trillion dollars a year. Not stolen. Just a split that moved.
The Labor Department tracks the same thing for private businesses. For decades after the war, workers' share barely budged. Then it started to slide. Today it's the lowest on record.

Why? Economists still argue. Global trade, a few superstar companies, and automation all get blamed. But here's what a robot adds. A robot is capital. When a machine does a task a person used to do, the money that paid that person now goes to whoever owns the machine.

scenes.narration: Dana gets it right away. Her warehouse didn't fire anyone this year. It just stopped hiring for the night shift. The robots took those hours. And the money those hours used to earn didn't vanish. It went somewhere.

So Dana asks the obvious question. Who owns the machines? Mostly, whoever owns the company. In other words, stocks. So let's line up every household in America, from the least wealthy to the most, and share out a hundred dollars' worth of the stock they own.
The whole bottom half of the country, all together, gets less than a dollar.
And the richest tenth of households? They get almost ninety. Nearly the whole pile.
Dana's neighbor Milo, a retired bus driver, has a retirement account from work. Accounts like his are spread wider than stocks. But even there, the poorer households hold only a sliver.

Now connect the dots. If robots move money from paychecks to profits, the money climbs this ladder, to whoever holds the shares. For generations, getting ahead meant getting a better job. When machines do more of the work, owning a piece of them could matter just as much.

And right now, the biggest machines in history are going up. Data centers for AI. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent more than six hundred billion dollars on buildings and equipment in the past year, by our sum.
Much of that money lands at the company selling the chips. In its latest quarter, Nvidia kept most of every dollar of sales as profit.
Let me draw the loop. A business pays for AI instead of hiring. That money goes to a cloud company. The cloud company buys chips and builds data centers. Profits flow to the shareholders of both.
Now notice who's missing from the loop. The worker whose task was automated. Unless that worker also owns shares.

Dana looks at the loop and sees herself outside it. Her pay comes from the warehouse. The robots come from someone else's factory, and they run on someone else's cloud. Every step of that chain has owners. She isn't one of them. Yet.
But it's a bet, not a guarantee. Some of this spending may never pay off. Over the past year, Amazon spent more cash than its business brought in. Owners get the upside. Owners also carry the risk.

So is AI already moving money from people like Dana to the owners? Let's separate what's been measured from what's been predicted. First, a finding. When a company gave its customer-support agents an AI assistant, they solved more problems per hour, and the newest, least experienced agents gained the most.
In Denmark, researchers matched chatbot use with official payroll records. Since ChatGPT arrived, they've found no measurable effect on pay or hours.

But in America, payroll data shows something to watch. Among the youngest workers in the jobs most exposed to AI, employment is almost a fifth below where it would otherwise be. Experienced workers show no such gap. The researchers call it an early warning, not proof.
Factory robots have a longer record. Economists found that American towns that added more robots saw fewer jobs and slightly lower pay.

Then there are forecasts. MIT economist Daron Acemoglu predicts AI will give productivity only a small lift over the next decade, and widen the gap between what capital earns and what work earns. That's a model, not a measurement. Forecasts differ widely.
And this has happened before. Britain, the age of steam. Machines multiplied what every worker could make. Factory owners grew rich. Workers' pay barely moved.

Economic historian Robert Allen measured it. Let me draw his story. Output per worker kept climbing. Real wages stayed flat. The profit rate doubled. Historians call it Engels' pause, after Friedrich Engels, who described the factory workers of Manchester.

Then, around the middle of the eighteen hundreds, wages finally began to rise with productivity. The pause ended. But it lasted decades. For the workers who lived through it, eventually came too late.

So are we living through a new Engels' pause? Nobody can say yet. Workers' share of business output is at a record low, but AI has barely reached most workplaces. What history does show is that the pause wasn't automatic, and neither was the catch-up. It depends on new jobs, new skills, and who gets to own the new machines.

Now, the other side. First, new jobs. A team led by economist David Autor found that most Americans today work in job specialties that didn't exist in nineteen forty. Machines take over tasks. New kinds of work keep appearing.
Second, productivity can lift pay. When things get cheaper to make, people buy more. And workers who use AI well can become more valuable. Like Dana, who now runs the robot fleet.
Third, skills still pay. A full-time worker with at least a bachelor's degree typically earns about three-quarters more than a high school graduate.

And fourth, policy can change the split. Some want to spread ownership wider, with employee ownership, accounts for kids, or public funds like Alaska's oil dividend, which we covered in another film. Others prefer training, or changing how work and capital are taxed. Others say markets will sort it out. Each has trade-offs. This film takes no side.

So Dana asks the practical question. What can an ordinary person actually own? Quick note. This is education, not investment advice. We're not telling anyone what to buy. Most American families own at least some stock, often through a retirement account. But among lower-income families, fewer than one in three do.

Let me draw the doors. The most common is a workplace retirement account, like a four-oh-one-k. Inside, many people hold index funds, which own small slices of hundreds of companies at once. Some employers offer stock plans. Employee stock ownership plans alone cover millions of people.

But owning isn't free money. Stock prices can fall hard and take years to recover. Fees eat returns. And betting your savings on your own employer, or on a single hot company, piles risk on risk. Owning a slice of the machines means sharing their bad years too.

As for Dana, she finally reads the benefits papers she'd ignored for years. Her employer offers a retirement plan, and she never signed up. That's her decision, not advice for anyone else. But it's the moment she realizes she could stand on both sides of the loop. Earning a paycheck, and owning a small slice of the machines.

So, who gets rich when robots do the work? On the evidence so far, mostly the people who own them. The shareholders of the companies that build, sell and run the machines. And in America, that's a group where the richest tenth hold nearly the whole pile.

But it doesn't have to stay that narrow. History says pay can catch up, after a delay. New jobs do appear. And ownership isn't a closed club. more than half of American families already own some stock, even if most own very little.
For generations, the big money question was, what do you do for a living? Dana's question now has a second part. What do you own?
